headlines.description: At least five instances of graffiti with hate symbols and hate messaging were reported in San Francisco on Thanksgiving, according to the app Solve SF, which gives residents an alternative way to report issues to the city. At least three of those instances were reported in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park, and at least two were reported in the Outer Sunset near Ocean Beach. All the reported instances featured red graffiti stencils of the words “White Power,” and all but one of those instances included stencils of swastikas. Patrick McCabe, the founder of Solve SF, was watching reports come in as he usually does on Thursday morning and noticed a pattern of repeated hate graffiti. “I saw that first one was on one of those barriers, and I think later in the day, I saw some others pop up, and the last one I saw was the one at Ocean Beach,” he recalled. McCabe said he’d seen similar hate-filled messaging at Golden Gate Park, but this time the messages seemed to have a more coordinated effort. “And to see it stenciled means that somebody made a stencil, went out there, and intentionally did this,” he said. “I think a lot of people were shocked,” McCabe said of the graffiti, noting that his app received multiple reports from each location throughout the day. He explained that through the app, those reports are automatically funneled to San Francisco city departments, and that instances of hate or offensive graffiti are prioritized for quicker action. By Thursday evening, it appeared that the graffiti in Golden Gate Park had been removed, though one instance on a wall at Ocean Beach remained. NBC Bay Area contacted the city’s Department of Public Works Thursday. The department said a crew has been dispatched to the graffiti and will “abate” the graffiti if it is still up. “We have zero tolerance for hate-based graffiti,” said Department of Public Works spokesperson Rachel Gordon. San Francisco Supervisor Alan Wong, whose district includes the Sunset, said he was saddened to hear about the graffiti in his district. “I want to make sure we send the message that this is unacceptable for our neighborhood and our city,” Wong said. “San Francisco is a place that respects diversity,” he emphasized. “Constituents — and anybody — can feel free to reach out to my office or Department of Public Works, and we will make sure we clean up any sort of graffiti like that right away,” he continued. San Francisco residents can report graffiti to 311 and, depending on the circumstances, to the police department as well.
